opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that inference and reinforcement learning are where the field's compute is shifting, and where our team has the deepest roots.

Most of us came out of the SGLang project, so serving models efficiently is something we've worked on for years. We've seen firsthand that as models get deployed at scale, the cost of running them, not just training them, becomes the dominant line item. Every improvement in throughput, latency, or memory efficiency at the serving layer turns directly into lower cost or a better user experience. That's a very concrete place to deliver value from day one.

Reinforcement learning is the natural next step, and it's tightly coupled to inference. In modern post-training, especially for reasoning and agentic models, most of the wall-clock time in an RL loop is spent on rollouts, which means generating huge amounts of samples. That's inference. If your rollout engine is slow or doesn't fit well with the training side, the whole pipeline stalls. So the same techniques we've built for serving, like prefix caching, efficient scheduling, and handling long and variable-length generations, matter enormously for RL. Treating the two as one system rather than separate problems is where we think the big efficiency gains are.

There's also a gap in the ecosystem. Pre-training infrastructure has been heavily invested in by the large labs, and much of it stays internal. But a lot of teams, from startups to enterprises to academic groups, now want to do post-training and RL on top of open models, and they don't have production-grade tooling to do it. They end up stitching together pieces that weren't designed to work together. We want to give them infrastructure that's open, fast, and reliable, so frontier-level techniques aren't limited to a handful of companies.

Finally, it's about focus. Infrastructure is hard, and trying to do everything at once is a good way to do nothing well. Inference and RL are where demand is growing fastest, where our expertise is strongest, and where the two problems reinforce each other. Getting that foundation right gives us a solid base to expand from later.

r001.rationale: The response discusses RL for reasoning and agentic models, but does not say that differing application requirements cause post-training RL to branch into specialized models.

r002.rationale: It links infrastructure to serving and RL needs across startups, enterprises, and academic groups, but does not connect a fan-out of post-training RL to broadly reusable infrastructure.

r003.rationale: The response describes inference and RL as coupled, but does not state that inference fans out more than post-training RL.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that inference and RL are where the compute is actually going right now, and where the gap between what the model can do and what the infrastructure lets it do is widest.

A few years ago, the center of gravity was pretrain. You scaled data and parameters, and the serving side was almost an afterthought. That's flipped. Today the frontier models spend a huge fraction of their lifecycle being served, and increasingly, being served inside a training loop. Reasoning models, agents, anything with long chains of tool calls, they all generate enormous amounts of tokens, and in RL the rollout phase is dominated by inference. If you look at a modern post-training run, something like seventy, eighty percent of the wall clock is just the model sampling. So if your inference engine is slow, your RL is slow, and your research iteration speed is slow. The two problems are really one problem.

That's also why it fits us. My background is SGLang, which started as a serving engine, and the key insight there was that the structure of the workload matters. RadixAttention, prefix caching, structured decoding, those came from asking "what does the program on top of the model actually look like?" RL rollouts are the extreme version of that. You have thousands of trajectories sharing prompts, branching, going through tools, with the policy weights changing underneath you every few steps. You need fast weight sync, you need the sampler and the trainer to speak the same language, you need to not throw away the KV cache every time the policy updates. That's an infrastructure problem, not a modeling problem, and most teams are still stitching it together by hand.

The other reason is that this layer is becoming open and shared in a way pretraining isn't. Not everyone will pretrain a frontier model, but almost everyone will serve one and fine-tune or RL one. So if we build the open stack that makes inference and RL cheap and composable, we're building something a very large number of people can actually use. And honestly, we want to stay close to the researchers. The fastest way to learn what the next bottleneck is is to be the thing their experiment runs on.

So we start there. Serving first, because it's the foundation, then RL on top of it, because that's where the demand curve is steepest. The rest of the stack can come later, once we've earned the right to build it.

r001.rationale: The response describes RL trajectories branching through prompts and tools, but does not say differing application requirements cause RL to produce multiple specialized models.

r002.rationale: It separately describes branching RL trajectories and RadixArk’s goal of building an open stack for broad use, but does not connect that infrastructure goal to RL branching into specialized models.

r003.rationale: The response does not compare inference fan-out with post-training RL or say inference fans out more.

astra-6.text:
We’re focusing on inference and reinforcement learning because they’re closely connected. Inference is how a model actually delivers value to users, so its cost, latency, and reliability matter enormously. And in reinforcement learning, a lot of the work involves having the model generate attempts, getting feedback, and using that feedback to improve. That makes efficient inference a foundational part of the training loop, too.

The workloads have different requirements. A user-facing application may need a fast response, while reinforcement learning may prioritize generating many attempts efficiently and keeping generation coordinated with training. But a lot of the underlying infrastructure is shared. So focusing on these two areas gives us a way to improve both how models are used and how they get better.

r001.rationale: It notes that user-facing and reinforcement-learning workloads have different requirements, but does not say those requirements cause post-training RL to branch into specialized models.

r002.rationale: It says the two areas share underlying infrastructure, but does not connect a fan-out of post-training RL to RadixArk’s aim of building broadly reusable infrastructure.

r003.rationale: It does not compare the breadth of inference fan-out with post-training RL or state that inference fans out more.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is that inference and reinforcement learning are closely connected. Inference is how a model interacts with users or an environment, and reinforcement learning uses those interactions to improve the model. So the infrastructure has to support that whole loop: generating responses, collecting feedback, and updating the model.

With reinforcement learning, you can spend a lot of time generating rollouts. That makes inference efficiency a training concern as well as a serving concern. If we can make that generation faster and use the hardware more efficiently, we can shorten the iteration cycle.

That’s why it makes sense to focus on them together. We want infrastructure that helps teams both deploy models efficiently and improve them through experience.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes inference and reinforcement learning as a shared improvement loop, but does not say that differing application requirements cause post-training RL to branch into specialized models.

r002.rationale: It mentions building infrastructure to support deployment and model improvement, but does not connect reusable infrastructure to a fan-out of post-training RL.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not compare the breadth of inference’s fan-out with post-training RL.
